clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis, now classified within the epidermolysis bullosa spectrum, caused by loss of the focal-adhesion protein kindlin-1.
Presents from birth or early infancy with acral trauma-induced skin blistering that tends to lessen with age.
Progressive poikiloderma develops on sun-exposed skin, with mottled pigmentation, telangiectasia and atrophy.
Diffuse cutaneous atrophy gives characteristic fine wrinkling with a 'cigarette-paper' texture, especially over the dorsal hands and feet.
Marked photosensitivity is typical in childhood, and mucosal involvement causes gingivitis, periodontal disease, oesophageal and urethral strictures and ocular problems.
Caused by biallelic mutations in the FERMT1 (KIND1) gene encoding kindlin-1, which anchors basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane.
There is a heightened lifetime risk of aggressive mucocutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, mandating lifelong surveillance.
Diagnosis rests on the clinical triad with immunofluorescence or electron microscopy showing a variable plane of cleavage and reduced kindlin-1, confirmed by genetic testing.
reference.pathophysiology: Kindler syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in FERMT1 (also called KIND1), which encodes kindlin-1, a member of the kindlin family of focal-adhesion proteins expressed predominantly in basal keratinocytes. Kindlin-1 localises to focal contacts at the dermo-epidermal junction where it cooperates with talin to activate integrins, linking the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix and stabilising keratinocyte adhesion, spreading, proliferation and polarity. Loss of functional kindlin-1 destabilises this actin-integrin coupling, so basal keratinocytes detach under mechanical stress; because the defect lies within the basal cell adhesion machinery rather than a single fixed structural component, the plane of blister cleavage is variable and may sit intraepidermally, within the lamina lucida or beneath the lamina densa, a feature that distinguishes Kindler syndrome from the other epidermolysis bullosa subtypes. Disrupted adhesion and impaired signalling also cause reduplication and disorganisation of the basement membrane, progressive epidermal atrophy and the poikilodermatous changes of pigmentary mottling and telangiectasia. Defective keratinocyte function contributes to abnormal photosensitivity and, over time, to chronic inflammation, mucosal scarring and stricture formation. The same disturbance of adhesion, proliferation control and wound repair underlies the strong predisposition to squamous cell carcinoma that characterises the disorder in adulthood.
additionalDifferentials: Other subtypes of epidermolysis bullosa, particularly dystrophic forms
Bloom syndrome and other poikiloderma-associated genodermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence antigen mapping showing variable cleavage plane and reduced kindlin-1
Transmission electron microscopy of perilesional skin
FERMT1 (KIND1) molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Regular dermatological surveillance with biopsy of suspicious or non-healing lesions
Dental and periodontal assessment and oral mucosal review
Endoscopic evaluation for oesophageal strictures and urological review for urethral stricture
Ophthalmological assessment for ectropion, conjunctival and corneal involvement
redFlags: A new indurated, ulcerated or non-healing lesion suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Obstructive urinary symptoms from urethral or anal stenosis
Severe periodontal breakdown with early tooth loss
Rapidly enlarging or bleeding cutaneous lesion in an adult with the condition
reference.prognosis: Blistering usually improves after childhood, but poikiloderma, atrophy, photosensitivity and mucosal strictures progress, and adults face a substantial risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma that is the principal determinant of long-term outcome. With diligent sun protection and cancer surveillance many patients have a reasonable life expectancy.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the disorder as a conventional epidermolysis bullosa subtype and missing the poikiloderma and cancer risk
Attributing skin fragility solely to trauma and overlooking the underlying genodermatosis
Neglecting long-term squamous cell carcinoma surveillance in adults
Failing to screen for and manage mucosal strictures and periodontal disease
Underestimating the importance of rigorous photoprotection from early childhood
references: Consensus classification of epidermolysis bullosa (standard reference)
management: Meticulous atraumatic skin and wound care, minimising mechanical and frictional trauma and managing blisters gently, as there is no disease-specific therapy
Rigorous lifelong photoprotection with sun avoidance, high-factor sunscreen and protective clothing to limit poikiloderma and skin cancer risk
Regular dermatological surveillance with prompt biopsy of non-healing or suspicious lesions to detect aggressive squamous cell carcinoma
Dental and periodontal care for gingivitis and periodontal disease, with regular oral mucosal review
Endoscopic surveillance and dilatation of oesophageal strictures and urological management of urethral strictures
Genetic counselling and family screening, reflecting autosomal recessive FERMT1 inheritance
Coordinated multidisciplinary care across dermatology, dentistry, gastroenterology and urology
